A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MPCache and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–H. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting, renumbering, and the additional checklist in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and XSUM performance, private-inference latency and communication measurements, and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 reports original task performance, private-inference measurements, component ablations, Needle-in-a-Haystack outcomes, and static-eviction sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The core eviction procedure, similarity approximation, clustering, index sharing, and Algorithm 3 remain unchanged. However, v1's head-parallel top-k optimization disappears from Table 1, Appendix B.5, and the corresponding ablation in v2. The PDFs do not establish whether this optimization was removed from the implementation or only from its description.

E1.justification: v2 adds QMSum to the evaluated LongBench datasets and introduces Needle-in-a-Haystack, testing recall of information inserted at different positions within long contexts (Table 5 and Figure 13). This adds a distinct controlled retrieval scenario. NarrativeQA and PassageRetrieval, also added to Table 5, were already evaluated elsewhere in v1.

E2.justification: Table 5 changes from full cache, SnapKV, H2O, and MPCache to full cache, StreamingLLM, DuoAttention, SnapKV, Quest, and MPCache. Thus H2O leaves this comparison while three comparators enter. Figure 10 adds ArkVale and removes the no-KV-cache baseline. The original LongChat comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Table 5 replaces LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and adds a 1024-token budget alongside 2048. Needle-in-a-Haystack introduces context-length and insertion-depth sweeps at 30% and 50% budgets. Section 5.4 changes the stated Figure 11 static-eviction ratio from 75% to 70%; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a position- and context-length-dependent recall stress test in Figure 13 and a HotpotQA static-eviction sensitivity analysis in Appendix F.3/Table 7. It removes the separate top-k parallelization ablation and the dedicated no-cache necessity experiment from v1 Appendix F.4. Existing hierarchy, layer-sharing, similarity-weight, and 2PC analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its results. v2 checklist item 7 explicitly acknowledges the absence of statistical-significance reporting, without introducing a different reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 replaces Table 5 with results under the new model and budgets, adds Needle-in-a-Haystack findings and ArkVale measurements, and adds static-eviction results: HotpotQA F1 is 31.16, 30.54, and 28.89 at 0%, 70%, and 75% eviction. No-cache and separate top-k ablation entries disappear. Matched LongChat and XSUM tables retain their values; the replaced model results do not establish same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The commonality definition, similarity bounds and linearization, protocol mathematics, security assumptions, and Appendix G reasoning are retained with equivalent notation and renumbering. The new Section 4.5 expands the informal security explanation but introduces no new formal proof or theorem.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a training-free MPC-friendly framework combining static eviction and dynamic selection with clustering, similarity approximation, and cross-layer index sharing. The abstract retains the same 1.8–2.01× latency and 3.39–8.37× communication reductions. Added experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 Section 6 newly acknowledges residual overhead relative to plaintext inference and failure when later queries require information from statically discarded tokens. Appendix F.3 explains the eviction-ratio choice using sensitivity results. Section 4.5 additionally clarifies that shared indices remain encrypted; the underlying threat assumptions are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds an MPCache code-access link in the abstract and checklist. It removes the model-architecture table and checkpoint links, the explicit five-shot XSUM designation, and the detailed head-parallel top-k description. Hardware, LAN parameters, clustering settings, and the reduced 1024-dimensional timing configuration remain documented, partly relocated to Appendix F.1.

R1.justification: v2 updates Table 1 and Appendix A with works including ClusterKV, HashAttention, HashEvict, LM-Infinite, Native Sparse Attention, and LServe. It also removes the blanket statement that the discussed eviction methods depend on attention weights and are incompatible with FlashAttention. The central positioning as a training-free hybrid method optimized for MPC remains.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable. v2 condenses background and setup passages, separates security analysis into Section 4.5, expands the conclusion with limitations, consolidates Appendix F, and adds acknowledgements and a conference checklist. Title, authorship, terminology, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a single-column format and extensively rearranges displays. Figure 9 changes from a two-row grid to one row; Figure 1 gains an inference schematic; Figures 10–11 change their displayed components. Table 5 expands substantially, new retrieval heatmaps and a sensitivity table appear, and the architecture and no-cache tables disappear.

improvement.justification: The retrieval stress test, expanded comparator coverage, and eviction-sensitivity table strengthen empirical support for the retained method. Explicit recall limitations and a code-access link improve transparency. These gains are tempered by the loss of some implementation and model-specification details, while statistical uncertainty remains unreported. The revision usefully improves validation without resolving a fundamental deficiency in the core method or its evidence.
